name: ChaLearn AutoDL Challenge 2019
description: This paper reports the results and post-challenge analyses of ChaLearn's AutoDL challenge series, which helped sorting out a profusion of AutoML solutions for Deep Learning (DL) that had been introduced in a variety of settings, but lacked fair comparisons. All input data modalities (time series, images, videos, text, tabular) were formatted as tensors and all tasks were multi-label classification problems. Code submissions were executed on hidden tasks, with limited time and computational resources, pushing solutions that get results quickly. In this setting, DL methods dominated, though popular Neural Architecture Search (NAS) was impractical. Solutions relied on fine-tuned pre-trained networks, with architectures matching data modality. Post-challenge tests did not reveal improvements beyond the imposed time limit. While no component is particularly original or novel, a high level modular organization emerged featuring a "meta-learner", "data ingestor", "model selector", "model/learner", and "evaluator". This modularity enabled ablation studies, which revealed the importance of (off-platform) meta-learning, ensembling, and efficient data management. Experiments on heterogeneous module combinations further confirm the (local) optimality of the winning solutions. Our challenge legacy includes an ever-lasting benchmark (http://autodl.chalearn.org), the open-sourced code of the winners, and a free "AutoDL self-service".
evaluation_method: accuracy / area under the learning curve (time-limited evaluation)
general_score_metric: area under the learning curve (AULC) / time-limited accuracy
typical_sota_score: varies by task and modality; roughly 60–95% depending on dataset
reputation: Well-known community challenge with an enduring public benchmark and open-source winners, frequently cited in AutoML/AutoDL work.
notes: Heterogeneous multi-modal tasks with hidden testbeds and strict time/budget constraints; not an LLM benchmark; results sensitive to compute/time limits and ensembling/meta-learning strategies.
